title: Introduction & Medavy Chapter 2 Audit Overview
text: Hi, I am Kehinde Alabi, and this video is about my fact-checking work on chapter 2 of the Med Harvey cancer textbook. Chapter 1 was mostly right. Chapter 2 was not, and the errors were not scattered. They came in clusters because a whole run of numbers had been lifted from one stale source. Chapter 2 covers five major sections: defining cancer and uncontrolled growth, the history of cancer research, the hallmarks of cancer, oncology terminology, and cancer epidemiology. It is one of the largest chapters in the textbook, and it took a careful, systematic review to work through. I reviewed 46 claims in the main tab, 134

title: Audit Breakdown: 46 Claims & 5 Core Sections Reviewed
text: Sentences in the AI-only tab, and eight editorial issues. Of the 46 main claims, 25 were confirmed true, 18 were false, and three were flagged for ambiguity. That is a much higher error rate than chapter 1, where most claims checked out. The biggest pattern I found was stale data. Six claims in the history of cancer research section all came from the same 2021 commemorative article and have not been updated for 2026 textbook. For example, the text says there are 71 NCI-designated cancer centers, but the current count is 74. It says about 100 targeted therapies have been approved, but the real number is now over 157. title: The Stale Data Problem: 2021 & 2007 Outdated Statistics
text: Epidemiology section. Three claims were pulled word for word from a 2007 WHO publication, making them nearly 20 years out of date. The numbers on obesity, occupational exposure, and hepatitis B have all changed significantly since then. Even in the AI-only tab, where the AI flagged sentences as not needing human review, I caught three errors. One reversed a well-known biological pathway. Another placed a 12th-century scholar in the 13th century. And a third garbled one of Hanahan and Weinberg's six hallmarks of cancer. These are exactly the kinds of mistakes that slip through without human review. Chapter 2, reinforce something I keep seeing in this work. AI-generated text tends to grab numbers from whatever source it trained on without checking whether those numbers are still current. For a medical textbook, that is not good enough. Every claim needs verification. Your turn. Here is the prompt. Take a

title: Uncovering Errors in AI-Generated & Automated Content
text: Document that quotes statistics and pick five of them. For each one, find the original source and check the data on it, not just whether the source exists. Tell me which numbers are current, which were true once and have since moved, and which you cannot date at all. Do not tell me whether the number sounds plausible. A stale number always sounds plausible. That is the whole problem. I am Kehind Arbital auditing the Med Heavy Cancer textbook for Humanitarian's AI. Chapter 2 is done. Thank you for watching.
